name: Bird's nest facial

card.summary: A skincare treatment and supplement tradition built on edible bird's nest, the dried saliva of swiftlets, which users apply or eat in the hope of firmer, brighter, more hydrated skin.
card.aka: Edible bird's nest; swallow's nest; yan wo
card.note: Bird's nest is a known food allergen and adulteration is documented.

quick.overview:
Edible bird's nest is a nest made of hardened swiftlet saliva, eaten in Chinese cuisine for centuries. Traditional Chinese medicine holds that it benefits health, especially the skin, and today it appears in facial masks, serums and drinkable supplements marketed for hydration, elasticity and brightening.

Laboratory and animal studies and a few small clinical trials point to effects on skin aging, inflammation, wound healing, barrier function and pigmentation. A 2024 review concluded that results are promising but that more human clinical research is needed to establish efficacy and safety.
quick.how: People use it as a topical product (masks, creams, serums) or as an ingested soup, drink or supplement. Cosmetic products often use a peptide or extract of the nest, while traditional preparation involves soaking and cleaning dried nest before cooking it with rock sugar or in soup.
quick.risks: Bird's nest is a recognized allergen: a review of food allergy in Singaporean children listed it as the most common cause of anaphylaxis requiring medical attention there. Wikipedia reports that dyed or counterfeit nests and nitrite contamination in some nests are known concerns, which has prompted authentication research and regulatory tracking.

lead: Edible bird's nest (EBN) is built by swiftlets of several genera from solidified saliva and has been eaten as a delicacy for centuries, mainly in soup. According to traditional Chinese medicine, nests promote good health, especially for the skin.[1] Bird's nest facials, masks and supplements apply that tradition to modern skincare.

A 2024 review in Archives of Dermatological Research examined EBN's potential cutaneous benefits across photoaging, anti-inflammation, wound healing, skin barrier enhancement and skin whitening. It reported promising in vitro, in vivo and preliminary clinical trial results, while calling for future human clinical research to validate efficacy and safety.[2]

The nest is mainly sialylated mucin glycoprotein; reviews attribute its reported biological activity to components such as sialic acid and describe anti-aging, immunomodulatory and antioxidant properties alongside quality-control and authenticity issues.[3][4]

chain: Nest extract or peptide applied to skin, or nest eaten
Reported effects on hydration, barrier, collagen-related and pigment pathways
angle.text: Users apply nest-based masks and serums, or consume nest drinks, to improve hydration, elasticity and radiance. The proposed route runs through nest components such as sialic acid and peptides, which laboratory studies report acting on skin aging, inflammation and barrier function.

paras: Nests come from several swiftlet genera. Harvesting once relied on limestone caves in Borneo, but since the late 1990s purpose-built nesting houses have largely replaced cave harvesting as demand grew.[1] Wikipedia gives the composition as roughly 60 to 65% protein, 30 to 35% carbohydrate and about 1% fat, with calcium, iron, potassium and magnesium; content varies with origin, bird diet and site.[1]
Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, dates the nests' use in medicinal soups to the Tang dynasty and notes that commercial swiftlet farming expanded from the 1980s.[5]

Traditional Chinese medicine regards bird's nest as beneficial to the skin, and beauty brands extend this to facial masks and serums.[1][2] The 2024 dermatology review lists photoaging, anti-inflammation, wound healing, skin barrier enhancement and whitening as the areas where EBN has been studied.[2]

A clinical trial registered as NCT07723508, evaluating a bird's nest peptide on facial skin condition in 40 participants, is listed as completed.[6] A second registered trial (NCT04997863) examines a sericin hydrogel sheet containing bird's nest extract for wounds and skin graft donor sites.[7]

The 2024 review summarizes in vitro, animal and preliminary clinical results as promising and says larger human trials are needed.[2] A broader 2021 review of EBN covers its nutritional composition, anti-aging, immunomodulatory and antioxidant activity, and the industry's authenticity problems.[3] A 12-week double-blind randomized controlled study published in 2026 examined metabolic effects of dietary EBN intake.[8] Grokipedia describes a 2022 placebo-controlled oral trial reporting improved skin elasticity and fewer wrinkles, though that account has not been independently confirmed here.[5]
Bird's nest is a documented allergen. A review of childhood food allergy in Singapore reported it as the most common cause of anaphylaxis requiring medical attention in that population.[9]

Wikipedia reports that white nests can be dyed to imitate red nests, that red nests may absorb nitrite and nitrate from nesting environments, and that Malaysia introduced microchip tracking after counterfeiting led to a halt in exports to China.[1] Researchers have published markers for rapid authentication of nests.[10]

timeline.event: Purpose-built swiftlet houses begin to replace cave harvesting as demand rises.[1]
A comprehensive review of edible bird's nest covers composition, activity and authentication.[3]
Archives of Dermatological Research publishes a review of EBN's potential cutaneous benefits.[2]
